'''Howard Henry Wieman''' is an experimental nuclear physicist specializing in instrumentation and detectors for high-energy [[nuclear physics]].<ref name=BonnerPrize /><ref name=APSfellow />

In 2015, Wieman ([[LBNL]]) and Miklos Gyulassy [[Columbia University|(Columbia)]] were awarded the APS [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]].<ref name="BonnerPrize2">{{Cite web |title=APS Bonner Prize |url=https://www.aps.org/funding-recognition/winners?t=Bonner%20Prize%20in%20Nuclear%20Physics&y=2015&af=false |website=Bonner Prize Citations}}</ref>

Wieman is best known for leading the team that designed the [[STAR detector|STAR]]
[[Time Projection Chamber]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Anderson |first=M. |display-authors=etal |date=1 March 2003 |title=The STAR time projection chamber: a unique tool for studying high multiplicity events at RHIC |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0168900202019642 |journal=NIM A |volume=499 |issue=2–3 |pages=659–678 |doi=10.1016/S0168-9002(02)01964-2 |arxiv=nucl-ex/0301015 }}</ref><ref name=starphp>{{Cite web | title=The STAR Detector  | url=https://www.bnl.gov/rhic/star.php | access-date=28 October 2025 | website=25 Years Since First Collisions at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider }}</ref> (TPC) which was used to discover a new state of matter, the strongly interacting [[Quark-gluon plasma]]. The discovery was made at the [[Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider]] (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory. The  STAR TPC was built in Berkeley,<ref name=airplane>{{Cite web | title=A STAR is Born | url=https://www2.lbl.gov/Publications/Currents/Archive/July-14-2000.html#RTFToC3 | website=Berkeley Lab Currents |access-date=28 October 2025 |date=14 July 2000}}</ref> installed at RHIC, and tested throughout 1998 and 1999. The first Gold-Gold collisions at RHIC<ref name=bnlbulletin >{{Cite web | title=BNL Bulletin | url=https://www.bnl.gov/bnlweb/pubaf/bulletin/files/2000/20000616.pdf | date=16 June 2000| access-date=28 October 2025 | website=RHIC Begins World's Highest Energy Heavy-Ion Collsions }}</ref> were recorded by STAR with the TPC starting on June 12, 2000 <ref name=firstevent>{{Cite web | title=Berkeley Lab Science Beat | url= https://www2.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/RHIC-first.html | date=19 June 2000| access-date=28 October 2025  | website=Quest for the Quark Gluon Plasma}}</ref><ref name=CernCourier>{{Cite web | title=CERN Courier | url= https://cerncourier.com/a/rhic-starts-producing-data/ | date=21 September 2000| access-date=28 October 2025  | website=RHIC starts producing data}}</ref> and the data were published in January 2001. <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ackermann |first=K.H. |display-authors=et al |date=15 January 2001 |title=Elliptic Flow in Au+Au Collisions at RootS = 130 GeV |url=https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevLett.86.402 |journal=Phys. Rev. Lett. |volume=86 |pages=402-407 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.86.402 |arxiv=nucl-ex/0009011 |bibcode=2001PhRvL..86..402A }} </ref> The Run 0 data showed significant elliptic flow in heavy ion collisions and indicated that the collision zone at RHIC energies is behaving hydrodynamically and with significant thermalization. This was a key step in making the discovery of a strongly interacting [[Quark-gluon plasma|Quark Gluon Plasma]]<ref name=APSnews>{{Cite web | title=APS News  | url=https://www.aps.org/archives/publications/apsnews/200506/rhic-liquid.cfm | date=April 2005| access-date=28 October 2025 | website=RHIC Detects Liquid State of Quark-Gluon Matter }}</ref><ref name=PhysToday>{{Cite magazine | magazine=[[Physics Today]] | last1=Jacak | first1=Barbara | last2=Steinberg | first2=Peter | title=Creating the Perfect Liquid in Heavy Ion Collisions | url= https://physicstoday.aip.org/features/creating-the-perfect-liquid-in-heavy-ion-collisions | date=1 May 2010 | access-date=30 October 2025}}</ref> and a perfect liquid<ref name=BNLnews2>{{Cite web | title=BNL Newsroom  | url=https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=110303#:~:text=%22The%20finding%20of%20a%20nearly,Chaudhari%2C%20Director%20of%20Brookhaven%20Lab | date=5 May 2005| access-date=28 October 2025 | website=RHIC Scientists Serve Up 'Perfect' Liquid }}</ref><ref name=CernCourier2>{{Cite web | title=CERN Courier  | url=https://cerncourier.com/a/rhic-groups-serve-up-perfect-liquid/ | date=18 April 2005| access-date=28 October 2025 | website=RHIC groups serve up 'perfect' liquid }}</ref> which was announced simultaneously in 2005 by [[STAR detector|STAR]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adams |first=J. |display-authors=etal |date=8 August 2005 |title=Experimental and theoretical challenges in the search for the quark–gluon plasma: The STAR Collaboration's critical assessment of the evidence from RHIC collisions |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0375947405005294 |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=757 |issue=1–2 |pages=102–183 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysa.2005.03.085 |arxiv=nucl-ex/0501009 |bibcode=2005NuPhA.757..102A }} </ref>, BRAHMS,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Arsene |first=I. |display-authors=etal |date=8 August 2005 |title=Quark–gluon plasma and color glass condensate at RHIC? The perspective from the BRAHMS experiment |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0375947405002770 |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=757 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–27 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysa.2005.02.130 |arxiv=nucl-ex/0410020 |bibcode=2005NuPhA.757....1A }}</ref> PHOBOS,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Back |first=B.B. |display-authors=etal |date=8 August 2005 |title=The PHOBOS perspective on discoveries at RHIC |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0375947405005282 |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=757 |issue=1–2 |pages=28–101 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysa.2005.03.084 |arxiv=nucl-ex/0410022 |bibcode=2005NuPhA.757...28B }}</ref>, and [[PHENIX detector|PHENIX]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adcox |first=K. |display-authors=etal |date=8 August 2005 |title=Formation of dense partonic matter in relativistic nucleus–nucleus collisions at RHIC: Experimental evaluation by the PHENIX Collaboration |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0375947405005300 |journal=Nuclear Physics A |volume=757 |issue=1–2 |pages=184–287 |doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysa.2005.03.086 |arxiv=nucl-ex/0410003 |bibcode=2005NuPhA.757..184A }}</ref>

The STAR experiment took its last event on February 6, 2026<ref name=Phys.org1>{{Cite web | website=Phys.org  | url=https://phys.org/news/2026-02-success-relativistic-heavy-ion-collider.html | date=9 February 2026| access-date=9 May 2026 | title=A smashing success: Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider wraps up final collisions}}</ref> making it one of the longest duration collider accelerator experiments ever undertaken.

== Education and career ==

Wieman received his bachelor's degree from [[Oregon State University]] in 1966 and his doctorate in 1975 from the [[University of Washington]]. His doctoral advisor was Isaac Halpern. He was a post-doctoral fellow at the [[University of Colorado]] and then spent the bulk of his career as a Senior Scientist at the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]].<ref name=NitschkeAward  /><ref name=LBLnews3>{{Cite web | website=LBL Newsroom  | url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2014/02/18/heavy-flavor-tracker-for-star/ | date=18 February 2014| access-date=30 October 2025 | title=Heavy Flavor Tracker for STAR }}</ref> At times, he also worked for and in collaboration with the [[GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research|Gesellschaft für Schwerionenforschung]] (GSI, Darmstadt). He retired from LBNL in 2011 but continued to consult on STAR projects until the TPC took its last event in 2026.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://inspirehep.net/literature?sort=mostcited&size=25&page=1&q=exactauthor%3AH.Wieman.1&ui-citation-summary=true | title=Inspire HEP exactauthor:H.Wieman.1 | access-date=11 November 2025 }}</ref>

At LBNL he was responsible for the design and installation of the Low Energy Beam Line at the [[Bevatron|Bevalac]] heavy ion accelerator and for the development of two generations of large [[Time projection chamber|Time Projection Chambers]] (TPCs). His first TPC was the EOS Time Projection Chamber at the Bevalac,<ref name=NationalArchives>{{Cite web | title=National Archives photo of the EOS TPC | url=https://catalog.archives.gov/id/39147370 | access-date=29 November 2025 | website=National Archives Catalog | series=General Records of the Department of Energy }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://cerncourier.com/a/the-time-projection-chamber-turns-25/ | title=The time projection chamber turns 25 | date=27 January 2004 }}</ref> which he co-led with Hans-Georg Ritter. Wieman then led the design and construction of a larger TPC for the [[STAR detector|STAR]] detector at the [[Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider]] (RHIC) at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]. He finished his career working with thin, high resolution, [[Active-pixel sensor|active pixel sensors]]. In particular, the Heavy Flavor Tracker (HFT) pixel detector for the STAR experiment was a ground-breaking device<ref name=BNLnewsroom3>{{Cite web | website=BNL Newsroom  | url=https://www.bnl.gov/newsroom/news.php?a=24657#:~:text=The%20HFT%20was%20first%20conceived,in%20the%20creation%20of%20STAR. | date=19 February 2014| access-date=30 October 2025 | title=Heavy Flavor Tracker for STAR }}</ref> It became operational in 2014 and was used to observe [[D meson]]s produced in heavy ion collisions.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Roberts Jr |first1=Glenn |title=Heavy Particles Get Caught Up in the Flow |url=https://newscenter.lbl.gov/2017/05/30/heavy-particle-flow-gold-atom-collisions/ |access-date=26 January 2023 |date=30 May 2017}}</ref>

Wieman is a [[List of fellows of the American Physical Society (1998–2010)|Fellow]] of the [[American Physical Society]],<ref name=APSfellow /> was awarded the LBNL J.M. Nitschke Technical Excellence Award in 1999,<ref name=NitschkeAward /> and received the APS [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics|Tom W. Bonner Prize for Nuclear Physics]]<ref name=BonnerPrize2  /> in 2015.
